title: Scientific writing, visualisation and public communication · Rung 1
subtitle: Writing a paper as an argument, and drawing a figure that tells the truth
coverLine: One idea per paragraph, honest axes, and a reader who can state your argument after one pass
subject: S58
author: Dr. Harsh Maheshwari

about.why: Most researchers learn to write by copying the papers they read, and those papers are an uneven model. This book treats a paper as an argument made to a reader with little time, and a figure as a claim that has to be true to its numbers. It teaches the sentence and the paragraph as the units of clarity, the number written with its unit and its count, and the plot with honest axes and nothing on it that does no work. The test it sets is simple to state: a colleague reads your draft once and can tell you your argument.
about.howToRead: Read Book 0 first, or at least the sections this book names as it goes. Then read this one in order: the paper first, then the sentence and the paragraph, then the figure. The book asks you to build one thing: one section of a manuscript or thesis, rewritten so that each paragraph carries one idea, and shown to a reader. Choose the section before you start, work on it as you read, and draw one figure for it when you reach the figures.
about.prerequisites: Book 0, in particular decimals and rounding (A3), percentages (A4), ratios (A5), units (B1), graphs (C5), average and spread (D5), reading a table and a figure (F1, F2) and the shape of an argument (F4). The mathematics is arithmetic with a calculator: percentages, ratios, and putting counts into a formula stated in words. No algebra beyond that, and no statistics beyond a mean and a standard deviation. You need a piece of your own writing to work on, such as a thesis chapter or a manuscript section, and any program that draws a chart; a spreadsheet will do if you are prepared to change nearly all of its defaults.

blurb: A short book on the first craft of scientific communication. It covers what a research paper is and why it is an argument rather than a diary of what was done, how to write the one sentence your paper exists to say, the sentence and the paragraph as units of clarity, how to report a number, how to cite a source, how to measure and cut a draft, how to make a table that stands alone, and how to choose, draw and caption a figure whose axes tell the truth. It ends with one real Indian survey result taken from a table to a paragraph and a figure a colleague can restate.

sections.title: What a research paper is: its parts and what each part is for
A paper is an argument, not a report of activities
The one message: your argument in one or two sentences, written first
The argument across sections: from the gap to the answer and its limits
Citing and referencing: the original source, in the order cited, in one format
The parts of a sentence a writer works with
The sentence as the unit of clarity
Words: the everyday word, one term for one thing, abbreviations that cost the reader
Numbers in a sentence: the unit, the count behind the percentage, and no more digits than the data hold
One idea per paragraph: the topic sentence, its support, and the reverse outline
Measuring a draft: words per sentence, a readability score, and what they cannot show
Cutting: deleting the words, sentences and paragraphs that do no work
Showing a draft to a reader: the one-pass test
A figure makes one claim
Choosing the mark: what the eye reads accurately, and the shape of the data
Show the data: when a bar of means hides what the points would show
Honest axes: where an axis starts, what range it shows, and measuring the distortion
Decoration that does no work
Colour: for meaning only, readable by everyone, and in grey
Words on a figure: axis titles with units, direct labels, and a caption that stands alone
Making a table that stands alone
Making the plot: from a table of numbers to a finished figure
Worked journey: One finding, from the fact sheet to a paragraph a colleague can restate
